reasoning: The two sets are near-identical in skeleton: the same brief, spec, architecture, the same 12 pipelines, the same 30-task M1 plan and the same dependency graph. B comes out ahead because of a number of concrete fixes and better-supplied packets. In B's contract, runlog types carry the config as plain data (`RunRecord.config: Mapping[str, object]`, Checkpoint methods as plain data). This respects the generated boundary `runlog → core`, which A breaks by typing `config: RunConfig` and `methods: Mapping[str, MethodConfig]`. B's fixtures say an "11-checkpoint 2,000-step" run folder, while A's still say "3-checkpoint", which no longer fits TRAIN-03's 11 checkpoints. B pins the 10-float snake observation layout. B's TC-17 tolerance is statistically sound (at most 4 of 20, P(≥5)≈0.003), where A's "at most 1 of the 20 seeds" fails roughly a quarter of the time under a correct test. B's spine tasks create the stub modules that thicken tasks later fill (stats.py, verdict.py, check.py, style.py). In A, the spine tells the builder to call "the stubs their thicken tasks name", but no task writes those files. B's packets include the types a spine actually touches (Transition, Checkpoint, Comparison, WorldSpec/TeamSpec, worlds.make); A's T09 and T17 packets leave them out. B's Scope lists every deferred requirement (REPLAY, CHECK-02/03, NOTES), and B drops stale routed open questions from pipelines.md. B also splits the fish stage along real dependency lines (one fish → many → local sight), each milestone with checkable Exits, and lists PL-03 and PL-06 so fish runs can be batched and evaluated. A's single M3 lumps all three variants together and leaves out PL-06 even though its Exit needs TC-25. B's weak point is that its milestone IDs run out of order (M5 and M6 sit before M4), which reads confusingly. B also mislabels stats.py and verdict.py as "(new)" in the T25/T26 packets after T17 has created them. Both sets share a few flaws: a 5-step World replay double driving a 2,000-step loop test, charts importing baselines and core in breach of the boundary list, and a stale contract Retired section.

Solid statistics design (paired permutation, Holm) and a well-chosen two-exit DQN check world
Dependency graph explains every edge, and spines all start from the interface task
weaknesses: runlog contract types embed train/methods types, which breaks the runlog→core boundary
Fixtures still describe a '3-checkpoint' run folder after the switch to 11 checkpoints
TC-17 tolerance 'at most 1 of the 20' makes a correct test flaky
Spine tasks point at stubs (compare, verdict, chart check/style) that no task creates
Fish stage is one large milestone, and its Pipelines column leaves out PL-06/PL-03
Several spine packets leave out types they need (Transition, Checkpoint, Comparison, WorldSpec)

strengths: Contract keeps runlog free of train/methods imports by storing configs as plain data
Fish stage split into one-fish → many → local-sight milestones, each with checkable Exits and the right pipelines
Spines create the stub files their thicken tasks fill, so the call path exists from the spine onward
Richer packets (T09, T17) contain every type the step touches; snake observation layout pinned
Statistically sound TC-17 tolerance; complete Deferred list in Scope; stale routed open questions removed
weaknesses: Milestone IDs run M1, M2, M3, M5, M6, M4, which reads confusingly
T25/T26 packets label stats.py/verdict.py '(new)' though T17 creates them
Same 5-step World double used for a 2,000-step loop test; charts imports baselines/core against the boundary list
Planned layout leaves out charts/check.py, style.py and evaluate/final/stats.py, verdict.py that the plan writes
